title: Babbage's Difference Engine
description:
Babbage's Difference Engine worked out tables of numbers using **only addition**. Build one in Python.

The trick is the **method of differences**. Take the squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Subtract each from the next and you get the first differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. Do it again: 2, 2, 2. For any polynomial the differences become constant after a few rounds (for squares, after two).

```
value   1   4   9   16   25
1st       3   5   7    9
2nd         2   2   2
```

So once the engine knows the first value and the first difference of each level, every next value comes from additions alone: add the 2nd difference into the 1st, then the 1st into the value. That is all the cranks and gears did.

Your program reads one line with the first few values of a polynomial (one more value than its degree, so three for squares), and a second line with how many table values to print. It prints the table, one value per line:

```
Values: 1 4 9
How many? 6
1
4
9
16
25
36
```

starter.main.py:
values = [int(x) for x in input("Values: ").split()]
count = int(input("How many? "))
for v in values:
    print(v)

solution.main.py:
values = [int(x) for x in input("Values: ").split()]
count = int(input("How many? "))

# The difference table: column 0 is the value, column k the k-th difference, all at the first position.
levels = [values]
while len(levels[-1]) > 1:
    last = levels[-1]
    levels.append([last[i + 1] - last[i] for i in range(len(last) - 1)])
engine = [level[0] for level in levels]

for _ in range(count):
    print(engine[0])
    # Turn the cranks: each column takes in the one to its right, starting from the left.
    for k in range(len(engine) - 1):
        engine[k] = engine[k] + engine[k + 1]

hints: Build the difference levels first: each level is the differences of the one above, until a level has one number left. The engine's starting state is the first number of each level.
To make the next value, update the columns from left to right: `engine[k] += engine[k + 1]`. Doing it left to right uses each column's old neighbour, which is what the real engine did.
requirements: Work out the starting differences from the given values (subtract neighbours, level by level).
Produce the table with **additions only**: no multiplication and no powers in the loop that makes the values.
A single value (a constant) is allowed: the table is that value repeated.

tests.name: Babbage's favourite, x squared plus x plus 41
